content: All levels of the healthcare system must be equipped with the necessary training and resources to ensure the effective application of trauma care protocols. This includes providing essential materials such as gloves, goggles, and water-resistant gowns, as well as ensuring the safe disposal of sharps and biological waste. These measures are critical across all healthcare settings, with water-resistant clothing being particularly important in hospitals where large volumes of bodily fluids may come into contact with healthcare workers during trauma resuscitation. While such protective clothing is considered desirable at the basic level, it is essential in hospital settings where severely injured patients are treated. The availability of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV using antiretroviral medications is also deemed desirable at all levels of the healthcare system. Invasive procedures discussed in trauma care guidelines must always be performed under sterile conditions to minimize the risk of infection. These guidelines emphasize the need for continuous evaluation and optimization of care for injured children, including the amendment of existing protocols to improve outcomes. Healthcare providers must possess specific skills to manage pediatric trauma effectively. These include knowledge of age-specific baseline vital signs, understanding the physiological responses to blood loss and shock in children of different ages, and familiarity with pediatric fluid and blood transfusion dosages for treating shock and hemorrhagic conditions. Providers must also be proficient in inserting pediatric intravenous cannulas, performing peripheral cutdown access, and establishing intraosseous lines. Pediatric-sized equipment is essential for trauma care, including intravenous cannulas, blood pressure cuffs, urinary catheters, nasogastric tubes, intraosseous needles, and weighing scales. Laboratory facilities must be capable of performing tests on small blood samples from pediatric patients. Additionally, monitoring growth and development to ensure that normal milestones are met, despite injury or physical impairment, is a critical aspect of pediatric trauma care. Training in trauma care is vital for all levels of healthcare providers, from village health workers to specialized hospital personnel. Skills for initial evaluation and resuscitation are necessary for all providers, while advanced operative management skills are required for hospital-based practitioners. Training programs should address the specific needs of rural, low-income environments, where general practitioners often perform a variety of surgical procedures. Incorporating trauma-related skills into medical and nursing school curricula, as well as postgraduate training, is essential to ensure that healthcare providers are adequately prepared to manage trauma cases. Continuing education is crucial to prevent the decline of cognitive knowledge and skills, particularly for practitioners who do not frequently encounter trauma cases. Such education also provides updates on the latest advancements in trauma care. Documented evidence shows that continuing education courses, such as Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS), improve the process and outcomes of trauma care. For example, in Trinidad, widespread ATLS training led to significant improvements in therapeutic interventions and a substantial reduction in mortality rates among severely injured patients. Various trauma care courses have been developed and implemented worldwide, each tailored to specific contexts and needs. These include: 1. Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS): A widely utilized course provided by the American College of Surgeons, focusing on the first hour of trauma care. It includes lectures and skill stations using mannequins and anesthetized animals. While established in many highand middle-income countries, its implementation in low-income countries is limited by high start-up costs. 2. National Trauma Management Course (NTMC): Developed by the International Association for Trauma Surgery and Intensive Care (IATSIC) and implemented in India, this two-day course addresses the initial emergency care of severely injured patients in low-income settings. 3. Definitive Surgical Trauma Course (DSTC): Also developed by IATSIC, this course is designed for surgeons and focuses on the operative management of complex, life-threatening injuries. It includes lectures, case discussions, and practical training on cadavers or anesthetized animals. 4. Essential Surgical Skills (ESS): Run by the Canadian Network for International Surgery (CNIS) in partnership with African surgical departments, this five-day course trains primary care practitioners in managing common surgical problems in rural hospitals. 5. Primary Trauma Care (PTC): Administered by the PTC Foundation and funded in part by the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists (WFSA), this two-day course trains healthcare professionals in the early management of severe trauma in rural hospitals. It also addresses disaster management and injury prevention. 6. Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) Trauma Course: Developed for rural hospitals in Ghana, this week-long course covers emergency and definitive trauma care tailored to the needs of low-income, rural African settings. 7. Trauma Nursing Core Course (TNCC): Run by the Emergency Nurses Association, this course is designed for nurses in emergency departments and includes training in airway management, ventilation interventions, and spinal immobilization. 8. Trauma Team Training (TTT): A collaborative course by the Injury Control Centre in Kampala, Uganda, and CNIS, aimed at creating cohesive trauma teams in under-resourced rural health centers. Promoting these courses and adapting them to local contexts can significantly enhance trauma care services. Countries should define which courses best suit their national needs, specific provider groups, geographic areas, or institutional levels. In some cases, developing new courses tailored to local requirements, as demonstrated in Ghana, may be necessary. Additionally, addressing barriers such as high costs and limited course availability can facilitate the widespread adoption of trauma training programs, ultimately improving trauma care outcomes globally.
